Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The five chapters are the five parts of LESSON["lecture"] in content/lesson-7.py, in their order, in the lesson's own words and examples: the lamp, television, fridge and phone against the book, chair and bicycle; the wall socket, the plug and the battery; the three safety rules; the paperclip and the paper at the lesson's own magnet experiment; and the lesson's record table of five things, with kitchen foil as the metal that is not magnetic.
title: Electricity and Magnets
subtitle: Grade 1 Science
objectives: Identify things that require electricity to work.
Explore, talk about and describe what happens when magnets approach and touch different materials.
Follow instructions safely when doing practical work.
Make predictions about what they think will happen.
Collect and record observations and/or measurements by annotating images and completing simple tables.

beats.say: Press a switch, and the lamp lights up. Electricity makes it work.
A magnet pulls a paperclip. It does not even have to touch it.

at.touch: does not even have to touch

beats.say: Some things need electricity to work. Some do not.
A lamp, a television, a fridge and a phone all need electricity.
A book, a chair and a bicycle do not.
Here is the test. What if the power went off?
The lamp goes out. But you can still read the book.
If it stops when the power goes off, it needs electricity.
Electricity comes into your house through wires.
The wires go to the sockets in the wall.
A plug takes it to the lamp. The lamp lights up.
A battery gives electricity to torches and toys.
So look for a plug on a lead, or a battery inside.
Electricity is very useful. But it can hurt you.
Rule one. Only plugs go into sockets. Never fingers or toys.
Rule two. Keep electric things away from water. Wet hands and electricity do not mix.
Rule three. If a wire is broken, do not touch it. Tell a grown-up.
A magnet attracts some things. Attract means pull towards.
Bring a magnet near a paperclip. The clip jumps across!
It jumps before the magnet even touches it.
Bring the magnet near paper. Nothing happens.
People often say a magnet sticks. But glue sticks.
Pull the clip off, and it comes away easily. A magnet attracts, and lets go again.
Test each thing, and write the results in a table.
The steel paperclip is attracted. So is the steel tin lid.
The wooden block is not attracted. The plastic cup is not.
Kitchen foil is metal. Predict: will the magnet attract it?
Test it. Nothing happens. Not every metal is magnetic.
Look at the table. A magnet attracts iron and steel.
Some things need electricity. It comes from sockets and batteries.
Only plugs in sockets. Away from water. Tell a grown-up.
A magnet attracts iron and steel. Not every metal is magnetic.
Now predict, then test, and see the pattern for yourself.
